meta.title: The AI Bubble Didn’t Pop. Hedge Fund Leverage Did.
meta.thread_line: 6 threads · hedge fund leverage unwind · contagion map · 2030 forecasts vs sold-out contracts · AI revenue and agents · portfolio and tokenization · jobs and consumer confidence

snapshot: Visser's call: **this is a hedge fund deleveraging event, not an AI bubble popping** — the S&P 500 closed the week only 2.7% off all-time highs.
Hedge fund leverage more than doubled since 2023 to record highs; he says it will never again reach that level, and the selling may run into hyperscaler earnings or even the midterms.
The damage sits in the crowded AI pair trade: Qs down 5.5% for the week while 350 S&P stocks rose and Europe, Mexico, Brazil and Canada were all up.
Contagion is now spreading from equities into credit (HYG vs IEF) and converts, which is when multi-strat pods really get hurt.
He dismisses 2030 forecasts from Gartner, Bain and a Barclays desk — Micron, ASML, Lumentum and Amazon report capacity sold out or contracted into 2028-2030.
Anthropic is on pace for 90-100B revenue this year vs 9B last year; agent workflows are used by only ~2% of companies, so he sees demand at a step-up.
The majority of his portfolio is now crypto; he still holds Marvell, Micron, Nvidia and Eli Lilly, and would rather own CoreWeave bonds than its equity.
Macro flag: consumer confidence at its lowest since 2013 and shrinking financials/tech payrolls point to a margin and politics problem, not a recession.

themes.status: DELEVERAGING UNDER WAY — HE SEES NO RETURN TO PEAK LEVERAGE
themes.title: Hedge fund leverage is the bubble that popped
themes.lead: Record hedge fund leverage, now being forced down by losses on the crowded AI trade, explains the selling, not AI fundamentals.
bullets: Fed/OFR data: hedge fund leverage was flat to 2023, then **more than doubled** to all-time highs through Q1; long-short equity runs close to two to one, and prime-broker leverage is also at record highs.
Leverage growth of 15% in hedge funds plus fast growth at broker-dealers; he puts hedge fund positioning at $14 trillion, vs 40-60B of CoreWeave debt spread over six years.
WSJ's illustrative numbers: $11B of equity running $45B of positions, about 33B borrowed — fine only while it's making money.

A $20B flagship AI fund fell 44% in a month in August; **Lone Pine** (Steve Mandel), which he calls one of the best non-multi-strat funds of the century, erased a 44% gain — over 55% gross after fees, a GFC-sized drawdown he calls "LTCM-ish".
Situational Awareness fell an estimated 60-70% before being bailed out; Goldman Sachs crowded hedge fund longs fell 10% vs the S&P in July and 15% over four months, unlevered.
His own thematic portfolio fell 11% last week, worse than any week in July, which "felt a lot like capitulation".

Why it won't come back: terminal value past three years is unknowable, so Sharpe ratios get harder, short-lockup funds can't survive drawdowns, and retail with AI tools now matches hedge funds' speed to ideas.

quote.text: CoreWeave, not a problem. Hedge funds, big problem.

themes.status: PAIN TRADE MAY RUN INTO HYPERSCALER EARNINGS / MIDTERMS
themes.title: Contagion is spreading from the AI pair trade into credit and converts
themes.lead: The equity hit is narrow, but credit and convertibles joining in is what makes this phase dangerous for multi-strat pods.
bullets: Week: Qs down 5.5%, S&P down 1.95%, IWM down ~3% (six straight down weeks for small caps), yet 350 S&P stocks rose; two 1% S&P moves after ~100 days without one; VIX jumped 25 points in a week but still closed below 20.
S&P up 12% and Nasdaq up 13% YTD; semis (SMH) still up ~50% YTD; the AI trade is ~25% of the market and the crowded long everyone shares.
Correlation break: the **Mexican Bolsa** went from near 52-week lows straight up while the Qs fell; fertilizer/crop-input and short-SaaS trades also unwound.
Credit: a long HYG / short IEF synthetic credit trade gave back all its summer gains in one week; he heard biotech was a major pod problem in September.

Converts (CoreWeave, MicroStrategy) were hit in a "waterfall", as giant AI capital raises — Broadcom and Google each over $100B this year, plus SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI — force holders to sell other assets.
Volatility: single-name vol exploded while index vol barely moved, so there is no S&P put that hedges a cross-sector AI book; the MOVE index stayed calm, keeping this an equity event.
Timeline: deleveraging could take another month; the pain trade runs into hyperscaler earnings, possibly the midterms, then a year-end snapback if he's right.
themes.watch: He says outright that knowing when hedge fund pain is done is very difficult; the timing is a guess.

themes.status: NOT A BUBBLE — SUPPLY SOLD OUT INTO 2028-2030
themes.title: 2030 doom forecasts versus contracts already signed through 2030
themes.lead: Bears forecast impairment five years out while suppliers report capacity sold out or contracted for the same period.
bullets: Gartner: over $3.5 trillion of AI infrastructure could face impairment by 2030; Bain: AI needs 6 trillion and comes up 800B short by 2031 — he has never seen a market care about forecasts that far out.

Contracts: Micron's signed agreements cover more than 35% of revenue through 2030; ASML expects supply shortages through 2028; Lumentum sold out of AI parts to 2029; Andy Jassy says Amazon's AI compute is sold out beyond 2028.

Nvidia guided to ~70% revenue growth vs ~40% expected; its 2029 street estimate went from ~305B to about a trillion, yet the stock is flat for a year and P/E on next year's earnings is ~15 (closer to 10 on high estimates).
CoreWeave is at this price for the fifth time; clients are Microsoft, OpenAI, Meta, Anthropic, Mistral and Jane Street — 'not strippers in Florida' getting subprime loans.
GPU rental for old chips holds up: per Zuckerberg on Cheeky Pint, even an H100 is worth more than a year ago; DRAM prices made new highs.
Dot-com was built for real future demand but had no money coming in; fiber took 7 years to build, and here we're in year two calling a bubble.
Hyperscaler stocks (Amazon, Meta, Google, Microsoft) made new all-time highs as a group, which he says argues against capital being the breaking point yet.

quote.text: If GPU prices are going higher, it's very hard to be bearish on CoreWeave

themes.watch: He grants capital is the biggest risk and CoreWeave's equity can keep building a higher risk premium; Jim Chanos' view that it may not be a good equity business stands.

themes.status: DEMAND STEP-UP FROM AGENTS AND SWARMS
themes.title: Lab revenue and agents say demand is still at a step-up
themes.lead: Exponential revenue growth and barely-started agent adoption make linear 2030 revenue forecasts unknowable, not bearish.
bullets: Anthropic is on pace for 90-100B revenue this year vs 9B last year; OpenAI + Anthropic finish ~170B combined, and a 600-700B forecast for them implies sharp deceleration already priced — in line with what David Sacks, Gavin Baker and Chamath said about six weeks ago.
AI capex could be close to $2 trillion, or 5-6% of GDP, next year; a16z says the labs added more revenue in 2026 than all of public software combined.
Adoption is early: per Andrej Karpathy few people are frontier users; an AI-engineer interview put agent workflows at ~2% of companies, and over 50% of agents in use are coding agents.
Aaron Levie: future tokens get consumed by agent swarms, which only started in the last two months; Patrick Collison expects personal agents to change how consumers deal with companies.
SemiAnalysis (Dylan Patel): 90 employees in 11 countries, from $20M revenue in 2025 to 100M now, while its own AI spend went from 100K a year ago to 10-11M by August.

Robotics: Unitree sold only ~11,000 robots this year (per Emad Mostaque) but says OpenAI's progress brings a GPT moment for embodied intelligence; he thinks distillation may be ending, widening the US-China model gap.
Brad Gerstner pressed Jensen Huang on when the build-out ends; Huang's one-word answer was "forever" — frontier labs are about a third of demand, with 500B a year for classical compute.

quote.text: If they just stay at the same level, they've won.

themes.watch: Revenue upside rests on markets (robotics, drug discovery, agents) he concedes haven't started yet.

themes.status: MAJORITY OF PORTFOLIO NOW IN CRYPTO
themes.title: Most of his money is in crypto, with a small AI book
themes.lead: He's moved most of his portfolio into crypto and believes the tokenized economy will dwarf public equity returns.
bullets: Still holds Marvell, a little Micron, Nvidia and Eli Lilly; the AI book is much smaller and "will never be as big as crypto again", though he may trade AI.
Bitcoin fell only 2.3% on the week while AI blew up; crypto index down 7% month to date; he expects no Bitcoin rally until hedge funds stabilize, and could see it meander toward the 75 area.
Thesis: dot-com built rails without demand; crypto is in the same spot, with demand coming from AI agents.
Tokenization will change covariance matrices and how margin is provided — he calls it the final stage of hedge fund deleveraging and plans to list something with his crypto.
Equities still earn returns for ~3 years, but private equity, private credit, VC, bonds and public stocks lose out to the tokenized digital economy (his Stripe-vs-Citi framing).
For the next 12 months he'd invest in AI agents and **Vera Rubin** agentic compute: a 15-name list cut down from 100, mostly optical.
Flags a crypto-related number: net interest income that could reach $107B next year, money he says is about to leave traditional markets.

quote.text: The majority of my portfolio moved into crypto. I'm very, very happy about that.

themes.watch: He is about to list a tokenized product with his own crypto, so the tokenization thesis is also his business.

themes.status: MARGIN AND POLITICS RISK INTO THE MIDTERMS
themes.title: Consumer confidence at a 2013 low as agent workflows hit jobs
themes.lead: The jobs market is weaker than headline unemployment shows, and agent adoption makes it a profit-margin and political story.
bullets: Consumer confidence fell to its lowest level since 2013, below the pandemic.
Jobs plentiful vs hard to get implies unemployment closer to 6%, like 2013.
Warren Pies: financials and tech payrolls are shrinking; excluding health care, jobs growth has been negative for about 18 months.
S&P earnings growth is running at 29% even as job creation slows, which he frames as a margin story, not a recession, though it could drive politics and the Fed.
Normal distribution of outcomes is breaking: losers (retail malls) lose growth to AI, winners (Amazon) compound, and middle names like banks drift toward losers.

takeaways.title: Read this selloff as forced deleveraging: watch HYG vs IEF and convert spreads for when it ends, not AI headlines.
Mark hyperscaler earnings and the midterms as possible ends of the pain trade.
Weigh supplier contracts (Micron, ASML, Lumentum) more than 2030 impairment forecasts.
If you want CoreWeave exposure at these levels, look at the bonds before the equity.
Keep compounding: $10 a month in the S&P for 50 years grew to about $478,000.

As far as I'm concerned, we have destroyed terminal value.
They are doing basic human linear garbage work. End of story.

other_news.title: Sources he recommends this week: Dylan Patel and Thibault (OpenAI) on Alex Kantrowitz; Zuckerberg and Alexander Wang on Cheeky Pint; Brad Gerstner, Jensen Huang and Clark Tang; Gavin Baker; Jared Kubin on quant flows and the Anthropic revenue math; *When Genius Failed* on LTCM.

Bears he names: Kuppy's oil/shale comparison (token price falls don't cut revenue the way oil prices do), Carl Quintanilla's bearish posts, and the media's misreading of Hock Tan's comments, which he says referred to guessing OpenAI's numbers, not AI investors gambling.
Misread news flow he lists: DeepSeek day, Liberation Day, Kimi, and CXMT's memory news hitting memory names until Elon Musk said the real problem is RAM supply.
Compounding: S&P returned 17% annualized over 10 years, 13% over 20, 12% over 30, 13% over 40; a penny doubled daily reaches $10.7 million by day 31; the S&P rose 16% over the last year.

Track record: worked through the 1994 Mexico devaluation at Morgan Stanley, LTCM's collapse, dot-com and the GFC, when he moved money out of banks into gold weekly; past drawdowns were ~60% (GFC), 50% (dot-com) and ~40% (COVID). Earlier analogies: AIG and Ciena charts, subprime mortgages.

Valuations: OpenAI and Anthropic went from under $100B two years ago to roughly $1.5-2T; he says they have won even if they stay there; SpaceX, Cursor and OpenRouter cited as private winners; Micron went from $10 to $80 and street desks missed it; new launches Grokbot and Meta's Muse.

glossary.def: Hedge funds running many independent trading teams under one risk budget, relying on low correlation across strategies.
Gross is total longs plus shorts; net is longs minus shorts. Multi-strats run high gross and low net.
Long high-yield bonds, short Treasuries: a synthetic trade that isolates credit spread exposure.
The value of a company's earnings beyond the explicit forecast window; he argues AI makes anything past three years unknowable.
His LTCM checklist: a correct thesis still fails on timing, volatility, financing, crowding, correlation breaks, liquidity or position sizing.
LTCM's bet that Brazilian Telebras preferred and ordinary shares would converge at privatization, a correct thesis wrecked by leverage and timing.
Nvidia's next GPU platform, the hub of the agentic compute names on his 15-name list.
